name: zmph (Zig Minimal Perfect Hash Map)
workload: Comptime-built minimal perfect hash map over string keys vs Zig's std.StringHashMap (runtime hash map) and std.StaticStringMap (binary-search static map); 100,000 lookup runs each, plus build-time comparison.
claimed_speedup: Lookup: zmph ~26ns avg vs std.StringHashMap ~45ns avg (~1.7x faster) and std.StaticStringMap ~10.4us avg (~400x faster, binary search). Build: zmph ~28.9ms is ~5x slower to build than StringHashMap (~6.1ms) and ~14x slower than StaticStringMap (~2.03ms).
compiler_and_flags: zig build benchmark --release=fast (Zig ReleaseFast optimize mode)
tradeoffs: Much slower to build (compile-time construction cost) than the stdlib alternatives; only worthwhile when lookups vastly outnumber (re)builds. Requires Zig comptime and a fixed, known-at-build key set.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (code is reference-only until a license is added). Benchmark is first-party (project author's own README), single machine, single run configuration reported (with percentile stats from zbench). Not independently reproduced elsewhere.

name: mph (cespare)
workload: Minimal perfect hash table (CHD algorithm, Murmur3 hash) built from a 102k-word dictionary; benchmark loops all keys doing table.Lookup vs an equivalent map[string]uint32 lookup.
claimed_speedup: Lookups take about 30ns and are 27% faster than a map[string]uint32 (BenchmarkTable-12: 29.99 ns/op vs BenchmarkTableMap-12: 40.92 ns/op); table construction from the 102k-word dictionary takes 18ms.
tradeoffs: Immutable/read-only table (no inserts after Build); values limited to what the CHD table format supports; construction cost scales with dictionary size.
caveats: First-party README benchmark; CPU model is stated but Go compiler version and build flags used for the reported numbers are not stated (go.mod only pins a minimum Go 1.17), so this is capped at Tier C per the project's-own-benchmark-with-partial-methodology rule. Not updated since Jan 2023.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars

name: QuickPHF
workload: Static compile-time-generated hash maps/sets built with the PTHash perfect-hash algorithm; divan micro-benchmarks compare per-key lookup latency and codegen/build time of quickphf's PhfMap/RawPhfMap against the phf crate's generated maps, across several key-set sizes (random u64 keys).
claimed_speedup: "about twice as fast as phf at lookup, and more than 10 times faster at construction" (README); RawPhfMap is faster still than PhfMap for larger maps. Exact per-size numbers are only shown in the benchmarks/lookup.png and generate.png charts, not as text.
tradeoffs: no_std, forbids unsafe code; RawPhfMap does not store keys (returns arbitrary answer on invalid query, so caller must guarantee key validity); requires build-time codegen via the separate quickphf_codegen crate.
caveats: Benchmark harness (Cargo criterion/divan benches) is public in the repo, but the README/benchmarks folder do not state the CPU model, OS, or rustc version used to produce the published charts, and the numeric results are only rendered as PNG/SVG plots rather than text, so exact figures could not be independently confirmed from the page text alone. Baseline is the phf crate (the Rust ecosystem's closest analogue to gperf/static perfect-hash tables), not Rust's std::collections::HashMap.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars (crates.io cross-reference)

name: lute
workload: Immutable maps/sets for fixed collections (up to 65535 entries), usable via macros or build-script codegen for compile-time construction; BENCHMARKS.md presents construction+search time, isolated query latency, and amortized per-query time vs the phf crate, on two CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark charts (construct-search, query-isolated, query-amortized) claim performance advantages over phf on both Apple M1 Pro (8-core) and AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, but the numeric values are rendered only as vector-graphic plots (matplotlib SVGs with text converted to paths), so exact ns/op or speedup figures could not be extracted as text.
tradeoffs: Limited to at most 65535 entries; keys must hash identically across build and target platforms (pointer width and endianness sensitive) when using compile-time-embedded maps, which affects cross-compilation portability.
caveats: Hardware for the benchmark is named (two CPUs), which is unusually good for a 4-star project, but rustc version/flags are not stated and the actual numbers are locked inside SVG plots (text rendered as glyph paths) rather than given as text/table, so this was capped at Tier C rather than A/B; could not verify exact claimed_speedup values.
